claims.text: The proposed Mg-transition-metal alloy will have a density below 6 g/cm³.
Sintering at 850–900 °C will stabilize a metastable, single-phase-like FCC/B2 microstructure in the proposed alloy.
The 850–900 °C window will suppress elemental volatility.
The proposed FCC/B2 microstructure will enhance oxidation barrier properties.
Sintering below 800 °C produces porous material because atomic diffusion is insufficient.
Sintering above 950 °C triggers phase segregation, including Laves or Heusler phases.
Sintering above 950 °C causes volatile loss of Mg.
Maintaining oxygen partial pressure below 10⁻⁵ atm will prevent stabilization of an α-HCP phase in the proposed alloy.
Sintering at 850–900 °C for a sufficient duration will produce greater than 95% relative density.
Kinetic control of diffusion and oxygen content at 850–900 °C will suppress Laves and Heusler precipitation.
Kinetic control at 850–900 °C will stabilize a metastable FCC/B2 solid solution.
At 850–900 °C, diffusion will be sufficient to homogenize the microstructure and eliminate porosity.
At 850–900 °C, the alloy remains below the thermodynamic threshold for detrimental phase separation.
A dense, single-phase-like structure will act as a barrier against oxidation.
In AlCoCrFeNi2.1, an FCC-L12 phase can act as an oxidation or corrosion barrier protecting an underlying BCC-B2 phase.
Relative density falls below 90% below 800 °C because atomic diffusion is suppressed.
Oxygen impurities stabilize an α-HCP phase.
Standard sintering at 1000 °C causes high volatility, phase segregation, and poor barrier properties in the proposed alloy.
Material sintered at 875 °C will have better oxidation or corrosion resistance than material sintered at 780 °C or 980 °C.

contradictions.description: The microstructure is called a single-phase-like FCC/B2 solid solution, but FCC and ordered B2 are crystallographically distinct phases; the cited FCC/B2 evidence likewise describes a two-phase lamellar microstructure rather than a single phase.
The boundary states that density failure occurs below 800 °C, whereas the baseline states that failure already occurs at 800 °C.
